course.title: How Computers Solve Problems
course.description: Write down a procedure precisely enough that something without judgement could follow it, then work out how long it would take.
course.audience: Someone who uses computers daily and wants to understand how a program decides what to do, without learning a language first.

paragraphs: A program is a list of instructions that a machine follows exactly, with no judgement of its own. Computer science starts from that fact. People study it because so much of what a computer does, from keeping a contact list in order to finding a route, comes down to writing out steps precisely enough for a machine and then asking how long those steps take.

The course has six lessons in two parts. The first three, Writing a procedure, start with lines that run one after another. They go on to choices made by a test, and then to steps that repeat in a loop. You follow small programs by hand, one line at a time. The last three, How long it takes, take the job of finding one item in a list and compare two ways of doing it, counting the checks each one makes as the list grows.
You don't need to learn a programming language. The programs are a few lines of Python-style code, and each lesson explains a line before it asks you to follow it.
outcomes: You'll be able to follow a short program line by line and say what x holds at the end.
You'll be able to say which branch of an if/else runs, including when a value sits exactly on the edge of the test.
You'll be able to count how many times a loop runs and spot one that will never stop.
You'll be able to count the checks a linear search and a binary search make on a list.
You'll be able to say how the number of checks grows with the length of the list, and when a sorted list is worth having.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with everyday arithmetic, and no programming experience is needed.

lessons.title: Steps a machine could follow

steps.headline: Steps with nothing left to guess

lead.text: Start with a card a machine could follow. Here is one: start with 8, add 4, halve what you have. Anyone who follows it ends up with 6. Nobody has to decide anything, because every step says exactly what to do and the steps come in a fixed order.

A card like that is an algorithm, a finite list of exact steps that ends with an answer. Finite means the list runs out. Exact means that no step leaves a choice open, so “add 4” counts and “add a bit” does not. A computer can follow only instructions that pass that test, which is why the first job in programming is to turn something you know how to do into steps that exact.
Notice that you also kept a running number in your head while you followed the card: 8, then 12, then 6. A program needs somewhere to keep that number too, and the next screen shows where.

steps.headline: A named place for the number

lead.text: A program keeps its running number in a variable, which is a named box that holds one value at a time. The name used in these lessons is x. Putting a value into the box is called assignment, and it is written with an equals sign.

The line x = 3 means “store 3 in x”. The line x = x + 2 looks odd if you remember equals from school, because no number is equal to itself plus 2. In a program the sign means store, and the line works in two moves. The machine first works out the right-hand side using whatever x holds right now. Then it stores the answer back in x.

afterFigure.text: Press Run code under the picture and move through the trace. After the first line the box holds 3. The second line reads that 3, adds 2 and stores 5. The 3 has gone, because the box holds one value at a time.
One line is easy to follow. A program has many, so the next question is which one the machine takes first.

lead.text: Think back to the second line of the last picture.

A program is a list of lines, and the machine runs them from the top, one at a time. Each line sees the box as the line before left it. Nothing runs ahead of its turn, and nothing runs twice unless a later lesson says it should.
That gives a simple way to follow any program by hand, which is called tracing. Write down what the box holds after each line, and use the newest figure for the next line.

afterFigure.text: In the picture x starts at 2. The second line adds 6, so the box holds 8. The third line doubles it, so the box holds 16. The doubling worked on 8 because 8 was what the line above had left. The 2 had already been replaced.
Tracing is the skill the rest of the course relies on. Try it on a program of your own.

lead.text: Write down the value of x after each line, and use the newest value for the next line.

reveal.text: You carried one value down the lines: 3, then 5, then 20. Each line used what the line above left behind.

steps.headline: The same lines in a different order

lead.text: The order of the lines is part of the program. Take two instructions, double x and add 1, with x starting at 5. Doubling first gives 10, so adding 1 afterwards gives 11. Adding 1 first gives 6, so doubling afterwards gives 12. Two different answers came from the same two instructions.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows both orders, one on each button. Each instruction works on whatever the one before it left, so swapping two of them changes what each has to work with. An algorithm is a list of exact steps, and the order is one of the things it has to be exact about.
Now try a pair where you can check the effect for yourself.

steps.headline: Run x = 3, then x = x * 4, then x = x + 2. What is the final x?

workedSteps.text: Line 1 stores 3 in x.
Line 2 multiplies the stored 3 by 4.
Line 3 adds 2 to what x holds now.

steps.headline: A new value replaces the old one

lead.text: So far each line after the first has used the old value of x in its sum. That is common, and it is not required. A line such as x = 1 does not read x at all. It puts 1 in the box and throws away whatever was there.

Take a program that stores 9, then stores 1, then adds 5. The first line puts 9 in the box. The second replaces it with 1, so the 9 is gone for good. The third line reads the box, finds 1 and stores 6. Nothing in the program remembers the 9, unless an earlier line had copied it somewhere else.

afterFigure.text: That is the second thing a trace has to follow. A line can read the box, and a line can overwrite it. When you trace a program, cross out the old value each time a new one is stored, so that you never use a figure that has already been replaced.

steps.headline: Find x at the end of x = 2, then x = x + 3, then x = x * 5.

workedSteps.text: Line 1 stores 2 in x.
Line 2 reads x, adds 3 and stores the result.
Line 3 reads the new x and multiplies it.
The box now holds 25.

lead.text: Decide which line stores a value without reading x, then carry on to the end.

reveal.text: The 7 was replaced on line 2, so line 3 never saw it. A replaced value is gone unless the program keeps it elsewhere.

lead.text: A procedure should add 1 to its input, then triple the result. This version has a slip in its last line: it adds 3 instead.

reveal.text: Repairing means finding the line that breaks the plan and then tracing again. You traced 4, then 5, then 15.

blocks.text: Ask a friend to make you a cup of tea and you can leave a lot unsaid. “Not too strong, with a splash of milk” is enough, because your friend knows what too strong looks like and how big a splash is. They fill in whatever you leave out.

A computer fills in nothing. It does exactly what each line says, in the order the lines are written. It has no idea what you meant, so a phrase like “a splash of milk” leaves it stuck, because it cannot decide how much a splash is. To get a machine to do a job you have to write the job down so exactly that nobody needs any judgement to carry it out.
This lesson follows one number through a short program, one line at a time. Along the way you'll see what a line like x = x + 2 does and what happens when two lines swap places.

intro.promise: By the end you'll trace a short program line by line and say why swapping two instructions changes the answer.

recap.keyIdea: A program runs one instruction at a time. Each line works on the value the line above left in x, and a new assignment replaces the old value.

blocks.text: Back at the friend with the tea, a machine needs every step written down exactly. You followed a number through a program as 3, then 5, then 20. You ran the same two instructions the other way round and reached 14. You saw 7 replaced by 2 before it could be doubled, and you mended a program until it finished at 15.

recap.nextHook: Every line so far has run, whatever x held. The next lesson opens with a café that takes £4 off a bill only when it is over £30, which is a line that looks at a value before it decides.

lessons.title: Choosing between paths

lead.text: The café rule has two parts. The first part is a test: is the bill over £30? A test like that has only two possible answers, yes or no. A program calls it a condition, which is a statement about a value that is either true or false.

The second part is what happens next. If the condition is true, the till takes £4 off. If it is false, the till leaves the bill alone. Each of these courses of action is called a branch, and only one of them happens for a given bill. Picture a path that splits in two, where the condition decides which fork you take.
Everything depends on what the test means. “Over £30” means more than £30, so £31 passes and £29 fails. A test is a precise statement, and a machine will apply it exactly as it is worded.

lead.text: Apply the café rule exactly as it is worded.

reveal.text: A bill of exactly £30 is not more than £30, so the test failed and nothing came off. You paid the £30 plus the £2 tip.

lead.text: A program writes the same choice with the words if and else. The line that starts with if holds the condition. The lines indented below it are its branch, and they run only when the condition is true. The lines indented below else are the other branch, and they run only when the condition is false.

afterFigure.text: Here x starts at 8. The test x > 5 asks whether 8 is greater than 5, and it is, so the machine runs the first branch and stores 18. The else branch is skipped completely. Press Run code and move through the trace to watch it happen. Then edit the first line to x = 3 and run it again, to see the other branch take over.
Indentation is how the program knows where each branch begins and ends, so the spaces matter.

steps.headline: Greater than, and greater than or equal to

lead.text: The test in the picture used >, which means strictly greater than. It leaves out equality, so 5 > 5 is false, because 5 is not more than itself. Programs have a second symbol, >=, for greater than or equal to. It includes equality, so 5 >= 5 is true.

The two symbols agree on every value except the one on the edge. For x = 4 and x = 6, the tests x > 5 and x >= 5 give the same answers: false for 4 and true for 6. They split only at x = 5 itself. The matching pair for going down is < and <=, which behave the same way at their edge.
That single value is where mistakes cluster, so a careful programmer tries the edge value first. Try a program with the edge value in it.

blocks.text: A café has a rule printed on the till: £4 off any bill over £30. The rule is short and the till follows it every time, with no argument. A bill of £35 loses £4. A bill of £20 stays as it is.

What the till does is look at one number and choose between two things to do. People make choices like that all day without noticing, but a machine has to be told exactly what to look at and exactly what to do for each answer. The tricky part is usually a number sitting right on the edge of the rule, such as a bill of exactly £30, where a careless wording gives the wrong result.
This lesson is about steps that ask a question before they act. You'll see how a program is written to choose, and what a single character does at the edge of the rule.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict which branch of an if/else runs, and say what changes when > becomes >=.

recap.keyIdea: A condition is true or false, and only the branch it picks runs. > leaves out equality; >= includes it.

blocks.text: Back at the café, the till's rule is now a condition with two branches. A bill of exactly £30 is not over £30, so it pays full price. You found that x = 5 takes the else branch with > and the if branch with >=, and that a doubling written after the test runs on both paths.

recap.nextHook: A test runs once and the program moves on. The next lesson opens with a bag of sweets, where the same test is asked again after every mouthful until something stops the eating.

lessons.title: Doing it again

lead.text: Plenty of jobs repeat one action. Washing a stack of plates is the plain example: while there are plates left, wash the top one. You check the stack first. If a plate is there you wash it and check again, and you keep going until the check finds no plates.

Programs repeat actions the same way, and a repeated action is called a loop. The loop's condition is checked before every pass. If it is true, the action runs once more. If it is false, the loop ends and the program carries on below it. Each run of the action is one iteration, which these lessons also call a pass, so the stack of plates took one iteration per plate.

The check always comes first. A stack that is empty to begin with gives no passes at all, because the very first check already fails. The number of passes is settled by the stack and the rule together, which is why counting passes is the main skill for the next few screens.

lead.text: Apply the rule to the bag, checking before every go.

reveal.text: The bag went 7, 5, 3, 1. At 1 sweet the rule failed, so you ate three times.

lead.text: In code the loop from the plates is written with the word while. The line that starts with while holds the condition, and the indented lines below it are the body, the action repeated on each pass. The machine checks the condition and runs the body if the condition is true. Then it goes back to the check.

afterFigure.text: Here x starts at 9. The check 9 > 5 is true, so the body runs and x becomes 7. The check 7 > 5 is true too, so x becomes 5. Now 5 > 5 is false, and the loop ends with x at 5. The body ran twice, but the condition was checked three times, because the last check is the one that fails.
That gap matters when you count. The number of passes is the number of checks that came out true, so a failed check never adds a pass. Press Run code and move through the trace to see each check.

lead.text: Count the passes, which are the checks that come out true. The check that fails is not a pass.

reveal.text: The body ran for x = 3, 2 and 1, then x = 0 failed the check. Four checks, three passes.

steps.headline: Trace x = 10, then while x > 4: x = x - 3. When does it stop?

workedSteps.text: Check 10 > 4: true. Run the body.
Check 7 > 4: true. Run the body again.
Check 4 > 4: false. The loop ends.
The body ran twice and x finished at 4.

steps.headline: Trace x = 0, then while x > 0: x = x - 1. How many times does the body run?

workedSteps.text: Line 1 stores 0 in x.
Check the condition before anything else.
Count the passes of the body.

steps.headline: Repeating a set number of times

lead.text: A while loop suits a job where nobody knows in advance how many passes there will be. Often you do know. If you want something done exactly three times, there is a neater way to write it, using range.

The expression range(3) hands out the whole numbers 0, 1 and 2. It starts at 0 and stops before the number in the brackets, so it never gives 3 itself. A for loop takes those values one at a time and runs its body once for each. Counting the passes then needs no checks at all, because the count is the number inside the brackets.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the loop variable i takes the values 0, 1 and 2 on the three passes. The body never uses i, so each pass does the same job. That takes x from 10 to 22. Use a for loop when the count is known in advance, and a while loop when a condition decides.

lead.text: Count the values range(4) gives, then apply the body that many times.

reveal.text: The body ran once for each value in the range: four times, adding 2 each time, so x grew by 8.

lead.text: A loop ends only when its condition turns false, so something in the body has to push the tested value towards that point. Take a loop that runs while x < 20, with x starting at 6. If the body adds 3, x climbs through 9, 12, 15 and 18. At 21 the check fails and the loop ends.

If the body subtracts 1 instead, x falls further and further from 20. The check stays true on every pass. A loop that never reaches a false check is called an infinite loop. The machine would carry on for ever, so the trace in this course cuts a run off after 100 steps.

afterFigure.text: When you read a loop, look at which way the body moves the tested value, and whether that is towards the point where the check fails. A body that moves the value the wrong way is the most common reason for a loop that never ends.

blocks.text: A bag holds 7 sweets and you set yourself a rule: eat two at a time, and carry on only while at least two are left. Each time you finish, you reach in for more.

The rule is the same each time you reach in. Each time you look at the bag first. If the rule allows another go, you eat. Nothing in the rule says how many goes there will be, because the bag decides that.

Programs repeat actions in just this way, and a machine never gets bored of it. This lesson looks at how a repeat is written and how to count its goes. It also looks at what goes wrong when a repeat has nothing to make it stop.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count how many times a loop body runs, and spot the change that would stop a loop from ending.

recap.keyIdea: A loop checks its condition before every pass and stops when it is false. Its body has to move towards that, or the loop never stops.

blocks.text: Back at the bag of sweets, the rule was a loop with a check before every go. You counted three passes as x fell from 3 to 0, and no passes when the first check failed. You saw range(4) take x from 1 to 9, and you changed a body so that a loop that never ended finally stopped.

recap.nextHook: You can now repeat steps. The next lesson opens with Maya and a pile of nine exam papers, where finding hers takes a loop that looks at one paper after another.

lessons.title: Looking things up

steps.headline: Looking at one item at a time

lead.text: Maya's method has a name. A search that looks at the items one after another, starting at the first, is called a linear search. The thing being looked for is the target, and each look at an item to see whether it is the target is one check.

The search stops in one of two ways. If a check finds the target, the job is done and the rest of the pile never gets looked at. If the checks run out of items, the target is not there. Nothing about the pile lets her skip ahead, so every item before the target has to be checked first.

That makes the cost depend on luck. If the target happens to be on top, one check does it. If it is at the bottom, every other item is checked first. The next screen puts a list on the screen so that the checks can be counted exactly.

diagram.alt: A row of six cards searched one at a time. In the lucky case the target is the first card and one check finds it. In the unlucky case the target is the last card and all six are checked.

lead.text: A computer holds the pile as a list: values stored in a row, each with a place number. The place number is the item's index, and indexes start counting from 0. The first item has index 0 and the second has index 1, so an item's index is always one less than its place in the line.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows a list of five values with their indexes beneath. Press Start search, then Next check, to watch a linear search for 12. It checks the 5 at index 0 and then the 12 at index 1, and it stops there. That was two checks, and the target's index is 1. The index counts from 0 while the checks count from 1, so the two numbers differ by one. You can change the number in the box to search for another target.
Both numbers are useful. The index says where the target sits, and the number of checks says how much work the search did.

lead.text: Count each comparison, including the one that finds the target.

reveal.text: The search compared 8, 3, 11 and 6, then stopped at the match. The 2 was never looked at.

workedSteps.text: Check the item at index 0.
Check the item at index 1.
Check the item at index 2. It matches, so stop.
The target is at index 2 and took 3 checks.
Compare the target 8 with the first item, at index 0.
How many checks does it take?

lead.text: Sometimes the target is not in the list at all, and a linear search cannot know that early. Suppose it has checked four items of a five-item list and found nothing. The fifth item might still hold the target, so the search has to check it as well.

The search can report a missing target only once the list has run out. An unsorted list gives no clue that lets it give up sooner, because nothing says any item is more likely to hold the target than another. A missing target costs a check for every item.
A target in the very last place costs the same, because every other item is checked before it. Try a search with a target that is missing.

lead.text: Search the list for 7, and count every check until the list runs out.

reveal.text: The search only learned that 7 was missing when the list ran out, so a missing target cost a check for every item.

lead.text: Because the cost depends on luck, it helps to ask what the most checks could ever be. That figure is the worst case: the largest number of checks the search could need for a list of that size, whichever target it is given.

For a linear search the worst case is easy to find. The unluckiest targets are the one in last place and the one that is missing, and each makes the search check every item. With 5 items the worst case is 5 checks, and with 12 items it is 12. For a list of any length n, it is n checks.

Worst cases matter because a program has to cope with them. A search that is quick when it is lucky and slow when it is not is still slow on the day it counts, so the worst case is the figure people quote when they compare searches.
Go back to Maya and her pile of nine.

reveal.text: If Maya's paper is last or missing, she has turned over every one. With no order to use, she cannot skip any.

lead.text: The list is longer now, so test the idea on it. The target is in the last place.

reveal.text: A last-place target costs as much as a missing one: a check for every item. For a list of n items, the worst case is n checks.

blocks.text: Nine exam papers lie face down in a random pile. Maya wants hers and has no idea where it is. The papers are in no order, so looking at one tells her nothing about any of the others.
All she can do is turn papers over one at a time. Sooner or later one of them is hers, unless her paper is not in the pile at all, and she has no way of knowing which until she has looked.

Looking for one item among many is one of the commonest jobs a computer does, whether the item is a name in a contact list or a word in a document. It takes time, so this lesson counts how many looks a search needs. You'll see what a lucky search looks like and what an unlucky one costs.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the checks a linear search makes when the target is first, last or missing.

recap.keyIdea: Linear search checks items in order until it finds the target or runs out. The best case is one check; the worst case is one check per item.

blocks.text: Back at Maya's pile, her method has a name and its cost has a number. Finding 6 took 4 checks and showing that 7 is missing took 5. Nine papers can cost her 9 turns. A last-place target among eight items cost 8.

recap.nextHook: Searching a pile checks every paper because the pile has no order. The next lesson opens with a number between 1 and 100 and a guesser who is told higher or lower, where order makes most of the checking unnecessary.

lessons.title: Halving the problem

lead.text: Make the game smaller. The number is between 1 and 10 and you guess 4. The reply is “higher”. That one word rules out 4 and everything below it. Only 5 to 10 remain, so a single reply removed four numbers at once.

A reply is worth most when the guess sits in the middle. If you guess 5 instead, “higher” removes 1 to 5 and “lower” removes 5 to 10. Either way about half the numbers go. A guess at the edge cannot promise that: a guess of 1 can only be right or be told “higher”, so it removes just one number.
All of this works because the numbers are in order, and “higher” means higher everywhere. The same trick can be played on a list, as long as the list is in order too.

lead.text: Now play the full game from the opener, with the numbers 1 to 100.

reveal.text: The reply “higher” ruled out 1 to 60 in one go. A search that uses order can discard whole blocks at once.

lead.text: Take a list whose values run from smallest to largest. A list like that is sorted, and the order is what makes the guessing game possible. The search compares the target with the item in the middle of the list, which plays the part of your guess. If the middle item is too small, everything to its left is smaller still, so the middle item and the whole left side can be thrown away.

If the middle item is too large, the middle item and everything to its right go instead. The search then repeats on what is left, using the middle of the smaller range, until it finds the target or has nothing left. This is binary search, and each comparison removes about half of the items that remain.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the middle of seven items is 18, which is too small for 31. So 18 and everything to its left are dropped. That leaves the top three items, and their middle is 31, so the search ends there. Two comparisons were enough, where a linear search would have needed six. Press Start search and Next check to watch the range shrink.

lead.text: Throwing away half the list is safe only because of the order. Take the list 9, 2, 7, 4, 6, which is in no order, and search it for 9. The middle item is 7, which is smaller than 9. In a sorted list that would mean the 9 lies to the right. Here the 9 is at the far left, so discarding the left side throws away the very thing being looked for.

That means a binary search on an unsorted list can miss a target that really is there. Sorting is the price of the method, since the list has to be in order before the search starts. With the order in place the saving is large, and the rest of this lesson counts it.

lead.text: Binary search shows that a target is missing by running out of items. Each comparison keeps a smaller range, and when no items remain the search knows the target was never there. Take the list in the picture and a target of 20. The middle, 18, is too small, so the range becomes 24, 31 and 40. The middle, 31, is too large, so only 24 is left. Then 24 is too large, and nothing remains. That was three comparisons.

One more rule keeps the counting the same for everyone. A range with an even number of items has two middles, and this lesson always takes the lower one, so the middle of 2, 4, 6, 8 is 4. Notice also how fast the ranges shrink. Seven items become at most three, and three become at most one, so a list of seven never needs more than three comparisons.
Keep only the half that could still hold 10, and stop when nothing is left.

reveal.text: The middles checked were 11, 5 and 8, then nothing remained. Three comparisons showed 10 is missing; linear search needs seven.

blocks.text: I'm thinking of a whole number from 1 to 100, and you have to find it. You guess 60 and I tell you whether my number is higher or lower than your guess. I always answer truthfully, so every guess gets a straight reply. Then you guess again.

Play it a few times and a pattern shows. Nobody plays by guessing 1, 2, 3 in turn, because each reply says something about a whole block of numbers at once. After a handful of guesses a number out of a hundred is trapped.
A computer can search the same way when its data is in order. This lesson shows how, and counts how many looks that saves compared with the one-at-a-time search from the last lesson.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the comparisons binary search makes on a sorted list, and say why it needs the list sorted.

recap.keyIdea: Binary search needs a sorted list. Each comparison with the middle item rules out half of what is left, so it needs far fewer checks than linear search.

blocks.text: Back at the guessing game, one reply to a guess of 60 left forty numbers. A sorted list gives the same kind of saving: 17 took 2 comparisons to find, and the missing 10 took 3 to rule out. In the eight-item list the last item took 4 comparisons, where linear search needs 8.

recap.nextHook: You have now counted both searches on lists of five to eight items. The next lesson opens with a sheet of paper folded in half again and again, which is the same halving run until the numbers get large.

lessons.title: When the input grows

steps.headline: A stack that doubles with each fold

lead.text: Go back to the sheet of paper. It starts as one layer. Fold it once and you have two layers. Fold it again and those two lie on top of two more, which makes four. The rule never changes: each fold lays the whole stack over itself, so the number of layers is twice what it was a moment ago.

A rule that simple is still surprising when it runs for a while. By the tenth fold the stack would be 1,024 layers thick. If each fold had added two layers instead of doubling them, the stack would have reached only about twenty. Doubling pulls ahead because every fold builds on all the folds before it.

Now turn the picture round. Start with that stack of 1,024 layers and cut it in half, then cut the half in half again. It takes the same ten cuts to get back down to a single layer. Binary search shrinks a sorted list in just this way, and that will let us count its comparisons without tracing every one.

lead.text: Start with one layer. Each fold doubles the stack, and you will fold it three times.

reveal.text: You doubled three times. Halving a range is the same process run backwards, which is why a search that halves its list gets through it so quickly.

lead.text: To say which of the two searches is better, you could time each with a stopwatch. The answer would depend on the computer, on what else it was doing and on which list you picked. A friend with a faster machine would get a different time for the same search, and neither of you would have learned anything about the search itself.

A better measure is the number of comparisons. Every search is a series of them: each time it looks at an item and checks it against the target, that is one comparison. The count is the same on any machine, so two people can compare it without arguing about hardware. It does depend on how long the list is, and the number of items a search has to work through is called its input size.

Earlier we found that linear search, in its worst case, makes one comparison per item, so a list with an input size of 7 can cost 7. Binary search halves the range each time. What we want to know is how each count changes as the input size gets bigger, and the rest of this lesson works that out.
Here is a sorted list with an input size of 7. Start with linear search, and count its comparisons for the target at the end.

reveal.text: Linear search compared every item in turn, so its count matched the input size. Next, see what binary search does with the same list.

lead.text: Binary search starts at the middle of the sorted list. Whatever it finds there, the middle item and everything on one side of it are ruled out, and the search carries on with the other side.

That gives a way to count, even though we can't know where the target is. To find the most comparisons the search could need, always follow the larger side that could be left. In the seven items in the picture, the first comparison removes the middle item and leaves three on each side, so at most three items remain.

afterFigure.text: Here the search is looking for 1. The middle item is 7, which is too large, so 7 and everything to its right are ruled out. That leaves 1, 3 and 5. Press Start search and Next check to watch it carry on. Next we'll write the sizes out for a list of 31, to see how the left-over range shrinks.

steps.headline: Find the most comparisons binary search needs for 31 sorted items.

workedSteps.text: Compare the middle of 31 items. The middle goes, and at most this many remain.
Compare the middle of 15.
Compare the middle of 7.
Compare the middle of 3.
Compare the last item. Nothing remains.
Count the comparisons. There was one for each line above.
Compare the middle item, 7. It is too small, so keep 9, 11 and 13.
Carry on with the range 9, 11 and 13 until the target is found. How many comparisons does it take altogether, counting the one with 7?

lead.text: Now take a sorted list of 15 items. As in the list of 31, follow the larger side that can remain after each comparison, and count until nothing is left.

reveal.text: The ranges searched were 15, 7, 3 and 1 items long, so four comparisons. A list of 7 needs 3, so doubling it and adding one item cost just one more.

steps.headline: How far a few comparisons reach

lead.text: The sizes we have been following suggest a pattern. Run the count the other way round and ask how long a list a given number of comparisons can deal with. A single comparison finishes a list of 1 item. With two comparisons the limit is 3 items, because the middle is compared and at most one item is left on each side. The limit for three is 7, since after the first comparison at most 3 items remain, and 3 is what two comparisons can manage.

Each limit is the one before it, doubled, plus one for the middle item. The numbers 1, 3 and 7 are each one short of 2, 4 and 8, which are the layer counts after one, two and three folds. After k folds the stack has 2ᵏ layers, so k comparisons cover at most 2ᵏ − 1 items.

This is the pattern of growth: how the number of comparisons changes as the input size increases. For linear search, doubling the input doubles the comparisons. For binary search, doubling the input adds a single comparison.

lead.text: The limits for one, two and three comparisons were 1, 3 and 7. Each is double the one before, plus one.

reveal.text: The limits run 1, 3, 7, 15. Each extra comparison doubles the length of list the search can handle.

lead.text: The pattern works at any size, so you don't need to trace a huge list by hand. Take a sorted list of 1023 items.

reveal.text: A thousand items cost about ten comparisons, where linear search could need a thousand. The stack of paper tells the same story: ten folds, 1,024 layers.

lead.text: Everything so far gave binary search a list that was already sorted. A list that arrives in no order has to be sorted first, and sorting takes steps of its own, many more than a single pass of linear search. Suppose that sorting a list of 1,000 items takes about 10,000 steps.

Take one search. Linear search on the list as it stands needs at most 1,000 comparisons. Sorting first and then using binary search costs 10,000 steps of sorting plus up to 10 comparisons, which is ten times as much. For a single search, linear search wins.

Now take 100 searches of the same list. Linear search could need up to 100,000 comparisons in all. Sorting once costs 10,000 steps, and each of the 100 searches then needs at most 10 comparisons, so the total is 11,000. The sort is paid for once and every search after it is cheap. Binary search pays off when the list is already sorted, or when many searches will share one sort.

blocks.text: Take a sheet of paper and fold it in half. You now have a stack two layers thick. Fold it in half again and the stack is four layers thick. Each fold lays the whole stack on top of itself, so the thickness doubles every time, whatever size the stack was before.

Paper gets too stiff to fold after seven or eight times, but a sheet that could be folded ten times would be 1,024 layers thick, and each extra fold would double that again. The numbers soon run far past what your hands can picture.

The last lesson ran this in reverse. Each comparison in binary search throws away about half of a sorted list, so a list loses its length as fast as the stack gains layers. This lesson counts the comparisons each search needs as its list gets longer, and then asks when sorting a list first is worth the effort.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the comparisons each search needs as a list grows, and say when binary search is worth it.

recap.keyIdea: Linear search can need one comparison per item. Binary search needs one more comparison each time the list doubles, but only if the list is already sorted.

blocks.text: Back at the folded paper, ten folds gave 1,024 layers, and ten comparisons cover up to 1,023 items. You counted 7 comparisons for linear search and 3 for binary search on a list of seven, then 4 for fifteen items and 10 for a thousand. For a single search of an unsorted list, skipping the sort was cheaper.

questions.prompt: Follow the three lines in order. What is x when the program ends?
hints: Follow the original program from top to bottom.
Start at 3, apply the addition, then apply multiplication to the updated value.
Do not apply both operations to the original 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Starting at 3, adding 2 gives 5, then multiplying by 4 gives 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. Each line works on the value the line above left in x: 3, then 5, then 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to run.
That multiplies first and adds second. Run the lines top to bottom, as written.
Line 3 multiplies what line 2 stored, not the original 3.

questions.prompt: What is x once line 3 has run?
hints: The multiplication now runs before the addition.
First calculate 3 × 4.
Use that updated value in the final +2 step.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Multiplying 3 by 4 gives 12, then adding 2 gives 14.

questions.onCorrect: 14. The same two instructions in the other order give a different answer: each works on the value before it.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 first, then multiplies. Here the multiplication runs first.
That multiplies by 4 + 2. Line 3 adds 2 to the value line 2 stored.
That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to add 2.

questions.prompt: Run the three lines. What is x at the end?
hints: An assignment replaces the old value of x.
The line x = 2 overwrites the earlier 7.
Apply the final doubling to the newly stored value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second line replaces 7 with 2; doubling 2 gives 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The second line replaced 7 with 2, so only 2 reaches the doubling.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the 7. Line 2 replaced it before line 3 ran.
Line 2 stores 2. It does not add 2 to the 7.
That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to run.

questions.prompt: Mend the last line so it triples x. Starting at x = 4, what does the repaired program finish with?
hints: Use the plan described above the program.
Start at 4, add 1, then multiply the updated value by 3.
Trace the repaired program, not the broken one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The repaired sequence gives (4 + 1) × 3 = 15.

questions.onCorrect: 15. Tracing the repaired program shows the plan working: add 1 first, then triple the result.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the broken version, which adds 3 to the updated x. The repair multiplies.
That triples first and adds 1 second. The plan adds 1 first.
That triples the 4 and skips the add. The plan adds 1 first.

questions.prompt: Trace x = 5, then x = x − 2, then x = x * 3. What is final x?
hints: Each assignment uses the value stored by the preceding line.
First update 5 by subtracting 2.
Multiply that new value by 3.
questions.onCorrect: 9. Each line works on the value the one before left: 5, then 3, then 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies before subtracting. Run the lines top to bottom.
That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to run.

questions.prompt: Which instruction stores a precise new value?
hints: A machine instruction must say exactly how to update the stored value.
Look for an assignment with a defined arithmetic operation.

acceptedIdeas: x = x + 1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The assignment x = x + 1 computes a new value from the current x and stores it. It gives a precise update the machine can execute.

questions.onCorrect: x = x + 1 is exact: it reads the current x, adds 1 and stores the result. A machine can follow it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Nicer” says nothing a machine could do. It needs an exact operation on x.
“A bit” is not an amount. A machine needs the exact change to make.

hints: Evaluate 5 > 5 before running either branch.
A strict greater-than comparison does not include equality.
Follow only the else branch when that condition is false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 > 5 is false, so the else branch subtracts 1.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The test 5 > 5 is false, so only the else branch runs and the if branch is skipped.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs the if branch. Check 5 > 5 first: is 5 greater than 5?

Test whether input 5 meets that condition.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the else branch. Is 5 greater than or equal to 5?
That is only the amount added. The if branch adds it to x.

hints: Run one branch, then continue after the if/else block.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The else branch changes 2 to 1, then the final line doubles it to 2.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The else branch made 1, and the last line runs on both paths, so it doubled that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x after the branch. The last line still doubles it.

Is 3 greater than or equal to 3? That picks the branch.
Apply that branch to the 3 you started with.

questions.onCorrect: 13. At the boundary, >= takes the if branch and adds 10. Test the exact threshold value first.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the broken version: 3 > 3 is false, so it subtracts 2.

acceptedIdeas: false

When that test is false, use the otherwise branch.
Divide the current 8 by 2; do not also subtract 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 < 5 is false, so the other path gives 8 / 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. 8 < 5 is false, so the else branch halves 8 and the subtract branch is skipped.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts 1. Is 8 less than 5?

questions.onCorrect: 3. The body runs once for each check that passes. The check that fails ends the loop without a pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the check that failed. A failed check does not run the body.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three doublings give 4, 8 and 16.

questions.onCorrect: 16. Each pass works on the last result: 4, then 8, then 16.

Continue after each mismatch until the list ends.
Count one value comparison for every inspected item.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All five values must be checked to establish absence.

questions.onCorrect: 5. A missing target costs a check for every item, because an unsorted list gives no order to skip by.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops one item early. The last item might hold 7, so it has to be checked.

questions.prompt: Search the eight items for 6. How many checks does it take?
hints: Find the position of 6 in the displayed eight-item list.
Linear search must inspect all earlier items first.
Count positions starting at one for the number of comparisons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The target is last, so all eight values are checked.

questions.onCorrect: 8. A last-place target costs a check for every item, the same as a missing target.

misconceptions.feedback: The target is last, so the final check is the one that finds it. Count it.
That is the value of the target, not the number of checks.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case number of value comparisons for linear search in 50 items?
hints: The target might be last or absent.
In either case linear search cannot stop before inspecting the last item.
Use one value comparison per item in the stated list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The target can be last or absent, requiring all 50 comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: 50. In the worst case every item is checked once, so the checks equal the list's length.

misconceptions.feedback: The last item still has to be checked, so count it.
Half is an average guess. The worst case is the most checks any target could need.

questions.prompt: What is the index of the fourth item in a zero-based list?
hints: Zero-based indexing labels the first item 0.
Write the index sequence for the first four positions.
An item's index is one less than its ordinary position.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The indices start 0, 1, 2, 3, so the fourth item has index 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The first item is at index 0, so the fourth is at index 3: one less than its position.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the position, not the index. Indexes start counting from 0.

questions.prompt: Search for 17. How many comparisons does binary search make?
hints: Start with the middle of the seven sorted items.
Is the middle value too small or too large for 17, and which half does that rule out?
The comparison that finds the target counts too.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: First compare 11 at index 3, then 17 at index 5: two comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The first middle rules out half the list, so the second comparison lands on the target.

misconceptions.feedback: The first middle is 11, not 17. The search needs another comparison.
That is how many checks linear search would need. Binary search discards half after each one.

questions.prompt: How many comparisons does it take?
hints: Find the initial middle element before discarding any range.
The target is 11.
If the first middle matches, no further comparison is needed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The initial middle value is 11, so the first comparison succeeds.

questions.onCorrect: 1. If the first middle is the target, no halving is needed. That is the best case.

misconceptions.feedback: Halving only follows a mismatch. Does the first middle match the target?
The search stops at the first match, so later halves are never needed.

questions.prompt: Search for 10. How many comparisons does it take to show it is missing?
hints: Keep only the half that could still contain 10.
After each comparison, list the items that remain and take the middle of those.
Stop counting when no candidate item is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The checked values are 11, 5 and 8: three comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Each comparison halved the range until it was empty, so absence needed only a few checks.

misconceptions.feedback: That is linear search, which checks every item. Binary search discards half each time.
After that many comparisons one candidate still remains, and it has to be checked.

questions.prompt: Search for 22, taking the lower middle each time. How many comparisons does it take?
hints: Use the lower middle whenever the remaining range has an even number of items.
After each comparison, write down which items are still possible.
Count every comparison, including the one that finds the target.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The search checks 10, 16, 19 and 22: four comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Each comparison halves the range, so even a last-place target needs far fewer checks than the list is long.

misconceptions.feedback: That is linear search. Binary search discards half after each comparison.
The search still has to compare the last remaining item. Count that one too.

questions.prompt: Must the list be sorted for this binary search to be correct? Answer yes or no.
hints: Discarding a half assumes the remaining values follow the same order.
Without sorting, a skipped half might still contain the target.

acceptedIdeas: yes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Order justifies discarding a whole half.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Order is what lets one comparison discard a whole half.

misconceptions.feedback: Without order, a small middle value says nothing about the half you would throw away.

questions.prompt: For seven sorted items, what is the worst-case number of value comparisons in this binary search?
hints: Count the largest possible remaining ranges.
Halve the remaining range after excluding the middle; keep the larger half for the worst case.
Each nonempty range requires one middle-value comparison.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The remaining sizes shrink from 7 to at most 3 to at most 1: three comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The largest remaining range shrinks 7, 3, 1, with one comparison for each.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts too few ranges. The last remaining item still needs a comparison.
That is linear search. Binary search discards half after each comparison.

questions.prompt: How many comparisons does linear search make to find 13?
hints: Linear search starts at the first item.
Where in the list is 13?
Count every item up to and including the successful comparison.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The target is last, so linear search checks all seven items.

questions.onCorrect: 7. The target is last, so linear search checks every item. Its count equals the input size.

misconceptions.feedback: The target is last, so the final item has to be compared too.

questions.prompt: How many comparisons does binary search make to find 13 in this list?
hints: The first comparison, with 7, is already counted for you.
Which item is the middle of 9, 11 and 13?
After comparing that one, what is left to check?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It compares 7, 11 and 13, giving three comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Binary search used the order to skip items: the same list and target, in under half the comparisons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is linear search on the same list. Binary search discards half the list each time.
Two comparisons still leave the target itself unchecked.

questions.prompt: What is the most comparisons binary search needs for 15 sorted items?
hints: After comparing the middle of 15, how many items can remain at most?
Do the same for that smaller range, and keep going.
Count each comparison until no items remain, including the one on a single item.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ranges searched are 15, 7, 3 and 1 items long: four comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Follow the larger side after each comparison, and count until nothing is left.

misconceptions.feedback: A range of one item still remains at that point, and it needs a comparison.
That is linear search. Binary search halves the range each time.

questions.prompt: What is the most comparisons binary search needs for 1023 items?
hints: The limits for 1, 2, 3 and 4 comparisons are 1, 3, 7 and 15. What come next?
Each limit is double the last, plus one. Keep going until you reach 1023.
Count how many limits you wrote down.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The limits run 1, 3, 7, 15 and so on, and the tenth is 1023, so ten comparisons are enough.

questions.onCorrect: 10. The limits double with each comparison, so a list of 1023 needs only ten.

misconceptions.feedback: Nine comparisons reach only 511 items, which is short of 1023.
That is linear search. Binary search halves the range each time.

questions.prompt: An absent target is searched for linearly in 1000 items. How many comparisons are needed?
hints: The target is absent, so a successful early stop cannot occur.
Linear search must rule out every listed item.
Use the total list length as the comparison count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Absence requires checking each of the 1000 items.

questions.onCorrect: 1000. A missing target forces a check of every item, so the count equals the input size.

misconceptions.feedback: The last item still has to be checked to be sure the target is missing.
That is an average guess. An absent target makes the search check everything.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case binary-search comparison count for 1000 sorted items?
hints: List the limits 1, 3, 7, 15 and keep doubling.
Find the first limit that reaches 1000.
How many limits did you write down to get there?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine comparisons reach 511 items and ten reach 1023, so 1000 items need ten.

questions.onCorrect: 10. Each comparison at most halves the range, and a range of 1000 takes ten halvings.

misconceptions.feedback: Nine comparisons cover at most 511 items, which is short of 1000.
That is the range after one comparison, not the total number of comparisons.

questions.prompt: A café takes £4 off any bill over £30. Your bill is exactly £30 and you add a £2 tip. How much do you pay in total, in pounds?
hints: Is a bill of exactly £30 over £30?
If it is not, does anything come off?
Add the tip to the full bill.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A bill of exactly £30 does not pass the test, so nothing comes off: £30 + £2 = £32.

questions.onCorrect: £32. “Over £30” leaves out £30 itself. A program makes the same choice, and has to be told which one it means.

misconceptions.feedback: The £4 comes off only for bills over £30. Is a bill of exactly £30 over £30?

questions.prompt: Why does the if branch run when x is 4?
hints: What does the = in >= allow?

acceptedIdeas: x >= 4 is true when x equals 4.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: x >= 4 is true when x equals 4.

choices.label: x >= 4 is true when x equals 4.
The if branch always runs first.

questions.onCorrect: The condition is true at the boundary because >= includes equality. That is the only difference from >.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither branch runs by default. The condition decides which one does.
4 is not greater than 4. The symbol is >=, not >.

questions.prompt: x is 7. Which condition is true?
hints: Which comparison allows the two values to be equal?
questions.onCorrect: x >= 7 includes the case where x equals 7. > and < leave it out.

misconceptions.feedback: A value is never greater than itself.
A value is never less than itself.

questions.prompt: Start x = 6. If x >= 6, subtract 1; otherwise add 1. Then double x. What is the final x?
hints: Test 6 >= 6 before changing x.
Run only the branch it picks.
The doubling runs after either branch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 >= 6 is true, so x becomes 5. The last line doubles it to 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. The test picks one branch, then the line after the if/else runs on every path.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the else branch. Is 6 greater than or equal to 6?
That is x after the branch. The last line still doubles it.

questions.prompt: A bag holds 7 sweets. You eat 2 at a time, and you keep going only while 2 or more sweets are left. How many times do you eat?
hints: How many sweets are left after the first time?
Keep going until fewer than two sweets are left.
Count the times you ate, not the sweets.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The bag goes 7, 5, 3, 1 sweets. You eat when 2 or more are left, which happens three times.

questions.onCorrect: 3. You repeated one action and checked the rule before each go. That is what a loop does.

misconceptions.feedback: You cannot eat two from a single sweet. The rule only lets you eat while two or more are left.

questions.prompt: Why does the loop stop when x reaches 4?
hints: What does the loop do before each pass?

acceptedIdeas: 4 > 4 is false, so the body is not run again.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 4 > 4 is false, so the body is not run again.

choices.label: 4 > 4 is false, so the body is not run again.
Loops always stop after two passes.
x can never be smaller than 4.

questions.onCorrect: The condition is checked before every pass. When it comes out false, the body is not run again.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing limits a loop to two passes. The condition alone decides.
x would go lower if the body ran again. The check before each pass is what stops it.

questions.prompt: When does a while loop check its condition?
hints: Does the check come before the body or after it?

acceptedIdeas: Before every pass.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Before every pass.

choices.label: Only after the body has run.
Once, at the start of the program.

questions.onCorrect: The check comes before each pass, so the loop can end as soon as the condition is false.

misconceptions.feedback: Then the body would run once even when the condition is false from the start.
It checks on every pass. Otherwise a loop could never stop.

questions.prompt: How many times does a for loop over range(3) run its body?
hints: List the values range(3) gives, starting at 0.

acceptedIdeas: Three times.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three times.

questions.onCorrect: The body runs once for each value the range gives, and the range stops before its limit.

misconceptions.feedback: Count every value range(3) gives, including 0.
range(3) stops before 3, so 3 is not one of its values.

questions.prompt: Start x = 19. While x > 6, subtract 5 from x. What is x when the loop ends?
hints: List the value of x after each pass.
Check the condition before each pass, not after.
Stop at the first value that fails the check.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 19 → 14 → 9 → 4. The check 4 > 6 fails, so the loop ends with x = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The loop kept running while the check passed, and ended on the first value that failed it.

misconceptions.feedback: The check 9 > 6 is still true, so the body runs again.
The check before the last pass fails first, so that pass never happens.

questions.prompt: I'm thinking of a whole number from 1 to 100. You guess 60 and I say “higher”. How many numbers could it still be?
hints: Which numbers does “higher” rule out?
Is the guess itself still possible?
Count the numbers above the guess, up to the top.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Numbers 1 to 60 are ruled out, so 61 to 100 remain: forty numbers.

questions.onCorrect: 40. One guess ruled out more than half the numbers. A search that uses order can discard whole blocks at once.

misconceptions.feedback: I said higher, not “right”, so the guess itself is ruled out too.
That counts the numbers ruled out. How many are left?

questions.prompt: Why can the search ignore 3 and 6 after the first comparison?
hints: What do you know about every item to the left of 9?

acceptedIdeas: The list is sorted, so they are smaller than 9, which is already too small.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The list is sorted, so they are smaller than 9, which is already too small.

choices.label: The list is sorted, so they are smaller than 9, which is already too small.
Binary search always ignores the left half.

questions.onCorrect: Order is what justifies skipping. Everything left of a too-small middle is smaller still.

misconceptions.feedback: They were never checked. The order of the list is what rules them out.
It ignores whichever half cannot hold the target. A larger middle would rule out the right half.

questions.prompt: The middle item of a sorted list is too small. Which items can be discarded?
hints: What do you know about the items left of the middle?

acceptedIdeas: The middle item and everything to its left.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The middle item and everything to its left.

choices.label: The middle item and everything to its left.

questions.onCorrect: In a sorted list, too small means everything to the left is smaller still.

misconceptions.feedback: Being sorted means every item left of the middle is smaller still, so they go too.
Those items are larger than the middle, so one of them could be the target.

questions.prompt: A sorted list holds 15 items. After one comparison with the middle item, at most how many items can remain?
hints: How many items are on each side of the middle?
The middle item itself is discarded as well.
Keep the larger side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The middle item has 7 items on each side. After the comparison, one side is discarded with the middle.

questions.onCorrect: 7. The middle item and one whole side go, leaving at most half of the rest.

misconceptions.feedback: That removes only the middle item. A whole side goes too.
That counts the middle item with a side. The middle is discarded as well.

questions.prompt: Maya's exam paper is in a random pile of 9 papers, or it may not be there at all. She turns papers over one at a time and stops when she finds hers. At most, how many papers must she turn over?
hints: What if Maya's paper is the very last one?
What if it is not in the pile at all?
With no order to use, can she skip any paper?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: If Maya's paper is last or missing, she has turned over all nine.

questions.onCorrect: 9. If the paper is last or missing, she has turned over every one. With no order to use, she cannot skip any.

misconceptions.feedback: After eight papers she still does not know whether the last one is Maya's.

questions.prompt: Why did finding 1 take 3 checks when 1 sits at index 2?
hints: What is the index of the first item? What number is the first check?

acceptedIdeas: Indexes start at 0, but the first check is check number 1.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Indexes start at 0, but the first check is check number 1.

choices.label: Indexes start at 0, but the first check is check number 1.
The index counts how many checks were made.

questions.onCorrect: The index is a position label that starts at 0. Checks are counted from one, so they run one ahead.

misconceptions.feedback: Each item is checked once. Nothing is checked twice.
An index labels a position. Checks are counted separately.

questions.prompt: Which item does a linear search check first?
hints: Where does linear search start?

acceptedIdeas: The first item, at index 0.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first item, at index 0.

questions.onCorrect: Linear search starts at index 0 and moves along one item at a time.

misconceptions.feedback: Linear search never jumps to the middle. It starts at the beginning.
It does not rank items. It starts at the beginning.

questions.prompt: Which target is a worst case for linear search on an unsorted list?
hints: Which targets make the search look at every item?

acceptedIdeas: One that is last, or not there at all.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One that is last, or not there at all.

choices.label: One that is last, or not there at all.

questions.onCorrect: The worst case is the target that forces every item to be checked: last place, or missing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the best case: one check finds it.
A middle target needs about half the checks, not the most.

questions.prompt: Two linear searches run on the same unsorted list of 6 items. The first target is in second place. The second target is not in the list. How many more checks does the second search need?
hints: How many checks does the first search make?
How many does a missing target need on 6 items?
Subtract one from the other.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first search takes 2 checks. The missing target takes 6. The difference is 6 − 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. A missing target costs one check per item. Finding the second item costs only two.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the missing-target search alone. The question asks how many more than the first.
That is the first search on its own. Compare it with the missing-target search.

questions.prompt: A card says: start with 10, subtract 4, halve what you have. Follow it in the order written. What do you finish with?
hints: Do the first instruction only. What are you holding after it?
Now halve what you are holding, not the 10.
Half of 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 − 4 = 6, then half of 6 is 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. You followed each instruction on the result of the one before. A program does exactly that, line by line.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves first. The instructions run in the order written, each on what the one before left.
That halves only the 4. The last instruction applies to everything you are holding.

questions.prompt: Why does line 3 multiply 5 and not 2?
hints: Which value is in x when line 3 starts?

acceptedIdeas: Line 2 replaced the 2 with 5, and line 3 reads what is stored now.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Line 2 replaced the 2 with 5, and line 3 reads what is stored now.

choices.label: Line 2 replaced the 2 with 5, and line 3 reads what is stored now.
Multiplication always uses the largest number the program has seen.
Line 3 uses the 3 from the line above it.

questions.onCorrect: The box holds one value at a time. Each assignment replaces it, and the next line reads the replacement.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in a program picks the largest value. A line reads whatever x holds when it runs.
The 3 was added to x on line 2. Line 3 reads x itself, which now holds the result.

questions.prompt: What does x = x + 2 do?
hints: The equals sign in an assignment means store, so what does the line do to x?

acceptedIdeas: Reads x, adds 2 and stores the result in x.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reads x, adds 2 and stores the result in x.

choices.label: Reads x, adds 2 and stores the result in x.

questions.onCorrect: The right side is worked out from the current x, then stored back as x's new value.

misconceptions.feedback: As a statement of equality it could never be true. In a program the equals sign means store.
A comparison asks a question. This line changes x.

questions.prompt: A program starts with x = 6, adds 1, then doubles x. What does x finish as if the two instructions swap places?
hints: Which instruction now runs first?
Double the 6 before anything else.
Now add 1 to what you have.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Doubling first gives 12, then adding 1 gives 13.

questions.onCorrect: 13. Swapping two instructions changes what each one works on, so it changes the result.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original order. Here the doubling runs first.
That is the add on its own. The doubling still runs, and it runs first.

questions.prompt: A sheet of paper is folded in half 3 times, each fold laid on top of the last. How many layers thick is the stack?
hints: How many layers are there after one fold?
Each fold doubles the stack.
Double the stack once more, and once more again.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One fold gives 2 layers, two folds give 4 and three folds give 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Each fold doubled the stack. Halving a range is the same process in reverse.

misconceptions.feedback: Each fold doubles the stack. It does not add two layers.

questions.prompt: Why compare searches by counting comparisons instead of timing them?
hints: Does a count change when you swap the computer?

acceptedIdeas: The count is the same on any computer.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The count is the same on any computer.

choices.label: The count is the same on any computer.

questions.onCorrect: A step count belongs to the procedure, not the machine, so it can be compared anywhere.

misconceptions.feedback: Time can be measured, but it changes with the machine and the run.
Counting is not faster. It is just independent of the machine.

questions.prompt: Why do at most 15 items remain after the first comparison?
hints: How many items are left once the middle one is set aside?

acceptedIdeas: The middle item goes, and the other 30 split into two sides of 15.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The middle item goes, and the other 30 split into two sides of 15.

choices.label: The middle item goes, and the other 30 split into two sides of 15.

questions.onCorrect: The middle item and one whole side are discarded. That leaves at most half of the rest.

misconceptions.feedback: It discards the middle item and one whole side, which is more than that.
Sorting is not part of the search. The comparison only discards items.

questions.prompt: What is the longest sorted list that binary search can finish in 4 comparisons?
hints: Write the limits for 1, 2 and 3 comparisons.
How does each limit come from the one before?
Apply that step once more after 7.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1, 3, 7, 15: each is double the last, plus one.

questions.onCorrect: 15. The limits run 1, 3, 7, 15, doubling and adding one each time.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the pattern in 1, 3, 7: how does each number come from the one before?
The limit is one short of a power of two. Which pattern do 1, 3 and 7 follow?

questions.prompt: You will search an unsorted list of 1000 items once. Suppose sorting it would cost 5000 steps. Which plan uses fewer steps in the worst case?
hints: How many steps could the linear search take at most?
Compare that with the cost of sorting alone.

acceptedIdeas: Linear search on the list as it is.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Linear search on the list as it is.

choices.label: Linear search on the list as it is.
Sort it, then use binary search.

questions.onCorrect: Binary search only pays off if sorting is already done, or will be shared by many searches.

misconceptions.feedback: The sort alone costs more than a whole linear search, so it cannot pay off for one search.

flashcards.front: Trace x = 6, then x = x / 2, then x = x + 4. What is final x?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The final value is 7.

flashcards.front: Trace x = 9, then x = 1. What is final x?
flashcards.back: The second assignment replaces the old value with 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The stored value is 1.

acceptedIdeas: true
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The test is true.

flashcards.front: Start x = 1. If x < 3, add 4; otherwise add 9. What is final x?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The final value is 5.

flashcards.front: Start x = 4; while x > 0, subtract 2. How many body executions occur?
flashcards.back: Two passes take x from 4 to 2 to 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The body runs twice.

flashcards.front: How many iterations does range(5) provide?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It provides five iterations.

flashcards.front: How many comparisons does linear search need when the target is absent from 12 items?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It needs twelve comparisons.

flashcards.front: What is the best-case comparison count in a nonempty linear search?
flashcards.back: One comparison finds a target in the first position.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The best case is one comparison.

flashcards.front: With lower-middle binary search, how many comparisons can a sorted list of 15 items require?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The worst case is four comparisons.

flashcards.front: What property lets binary search discard half the remaining items?
flashcards.back: The list is sorted in the comparison order.

acceptedIdeas: sorted
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The list must be sorted.

flashcards.front: What is the worst-case binary-search comparison count for 31 sorted items?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It takes at most five comparisons.

flashcards.front: What is the worst-case linear-search comparison count for 31 items?
flashcards.back: Thirty-one: every item may need checking.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It can take thirty-one comparisons.

courseChecks.title: Find your starting point
courseChecks.description: Six problems about instructions and searches. Trace each case, then see which lessons will help.

question.prompt: What is x after the last assignment?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The assignments store 6, then 10, then 30. Multiplication uses the value stored by the preceding line.

question.prompt: Which value is stored in x when this program ends?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 < 12 is false. Only the else branch runs, storing 12 + 3 = 15.

question.prompt: After all five iterations, what is x?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: range(5) produces five iterations. Starting from 1 and adding 3 five times gives 16.

question.prompt: Linear search starts at the left and stops at its first match. How many value checks find 8?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It inspects 14, 6, 2, 19 and then 8. The target has index 4, but finding it takes 5 value checks.

question.prompt: Using the lower middle each time, how many value checks does binary search need to find 31?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inspected values are 14, then 24, then 31. After each mismatch, the sorted order rules out the lower half.

question.prompt: For 63 already-sorted items with direct access, what is the worst-case number of binary-search value checks?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At most 6 value checks are needed: floor(log₂ 63) + 1 = 6. Sorting and access costs are excluded by the question.

courseChecks.title: Bring it together
courseChecks.description: Combine sequencing, boundary checks and search costs. Results appear after all six responses.

question.prompt: How many times is the while condition tested, including the final false test?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The condition is tested at x = 11, 8, 5 and 2. The first three tests run the body; the fourth is false.

question.prompt: The first value is overwritten. What is the final x?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second line replaces 13 with 4. The remaining assignments store 20 and then 14.

question.prompt: One lookup is needed. Count all the measured comparisons shown. Which plan uses fewer?

acceptedIdeas: Linear search: 20 total
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Linear search uses 0 + 20 = 20 comparisons. Sorting then searching uses 50 + 5 = 55; the small lookup count excludes its preparation.

question.prompt: This rule should double x when its starting value is at least 10. Which replacement fixes the comparison?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: x >= 10 includes the boundary and every larger value. Equality alone would fail for values above 10.

question.prompt: How many value checks does a full linear search need to establish that 9 is absent?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: None of the six entries is 9. With no ordering shortcut, the search must check all six.

question.prompt: Use the lower middle and stop when the candidate interval is empty. How many checks establish that 20 is absent?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The search checks 13, 22, 16 and 19. No candidates remain between 19 and 22, so it reports absence after four checks.

question.prompt: A packing routine changes the number of available slots. What value remains?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The routine expands 3 slots to 12 and then reserves 2, leaving 10.

question.prompt: A catalogue is stored in the order shown. Starting at the left, how many entries must linear search inspect to find 23?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 23 is the ninth entry, at zero-based index 8. The search inspects nine entries.

question.prompt: A delivery routine uses this boundary rule. What charge does it calculate?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 <= 4 is true, so the first branch keeps charge at 7. The else branch does not run.

question.prompt: An index contains 256 sorted records. With direct access and the lower-middle rule, what is the maximum number of binary-search value checks?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The bound is floor(log₂ 256) + 1 = 9 value checks. The longest route can include a final one-record interval.

question.prompt: Orders are shipped in groups of five while at least five remain. How many are left after this routine?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two iterations change 14 to 9 and then 4. At 4, the condition is false and shipping stops.

question.prompt: Can the usual binary-search discard rule safely find identifiers in this order?

acceptedIdeas: No; the values must be sorted using the comparison order.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Distinct values do not guarantee that discarded positions are too small or too large. Sorting by the same comparison order supplies that guarantee.
